I am always perplexed by why BWF purists feel the need to measure up against weight lifters at lifting weights.

As a result, BWF practitioners are by default adept at party tricks to try to impress weight lifters, rather than being primarily adept at things like running, jumping, kicking, climbing, tumbling, fighting, playing sports.

It seems like a tremendous waste. BWF should be about using your body well, and if you still have something to prove to weight lifters you may as well do something like Starting Strength on the side while continuing BWF, getting the best of both worlds.

The BWF community should really decontaminate itself of "Get a big bench just do fancy pushups! lol silly weight lifters" mentality, just like the parkour community should purge itself of people doing flips in the park and return focus to climbing, escape and evasion like in the old days.

You have an interesting viewpoint. I'm not a pure strength athlete, but I still want to make sure that I'm using my body better than the squats and oats crowd and that includes being able to out-lift them. Barbells are a well tested method of demonstrating raw strength, and if bodyweight work improves the ability to lift weights as well as actually lifting weights, then it's a pretty good endorsement of calisthenics. If I wanted to do Ninja Warrior type stuff, I would certainly practice the running, jumping, wall splits, etc. but my primary focus would be to build enough strength to move myself around effectively. General adaption > Specific adaption.

If you've read Starting Strength, I'm sure you've seen the arguments for strength having the most carryover in sports performance and general health. He even goes as far as to call strength the most important trait you could have in life. While he gets a little weird about it, he's right about the sports performance part. So the number one trait non-bodybuilders should be training for is strength, which is what those elaborate "party tricks" are for.

I don't know much about parkour, but escape and evasion sounds a lot more useful, fun, and impressive, so I'm with you there. You should still be really strong when you're trying to do those things though. I mean, Rambo was pretty swole...

TL,DR: I do Ross Enamait stuff and think it's the way to go

Parkour does require a lot of strength, specifically relative strength. Getting yourself over a wall is mostly about having strong pull ups plus good grip/traction, at least in my experience.

The way I see it, if a person wants to get strong past a certain point, they should simply use barbells on the grounds that it will be simpler and more effective.

High levels of strength can be built using calisthenics, but past a certain point it will require diminishing returns levels of creativity and effort.

For example, I have heard people recommend back levers as a way to build a heavy deadlift without deadlifting. In this hypothetical, that would work if and only if you also managed to train your quads, hamstrings, groin, glutes, traps and grip to the same degree, so right there one barbell exercise requires a minimum of 7 calisthenic exercises to equal, assuming there's not something else missing, and at that point we're still not sure how many pounds of deadlift per time spent on calisthenics we're getting. Huge input for diminishing returns reward. Potentially doable, but increasingly complex and time consuming and thus increasingly unlikely for most people.

I still very much utilize calisthenics, but I do so with conditioning and athletics in mind. For me it's about circuits of simple exercises like push ups/rows/lunges/V-ups, footwork drills, repeatedly climbing up a wall and jumping down again, shadow boxing to a tabata timer, etcetera. Since I have access to a barbell, I use that to improve my overall strength. I believe that approach is simple and effective, and allows me to use calisthenics for what they are actually good for rather than trying to make it another feat of strength, which seems to me like trying to pound nails with a hack saw.

Now of course all this goes out the window if a person has no barbell access, but that in my view is what improvised equipment is for. Isometric devices to approximate barbell moves at high effort, DIY concrete kettlebells and the like. I've estimated that making DIY concrete weights and using a thick round piece of wood for a barbell, any of us could make a weight set for approximately 10 cents a pound, and a wood & concrete squat rack for about $20. If even that is unavailable for whatever reason (which would be a pretty perplexing life situation, prison etc), then and only then do I see the pure calisthenics strength approach as most efficient.

Barbells are simpler and more effective right now due to a lack of good BW training programs. There certainly is a complexity issue with BWF, but if you had a bunch of amateurs build a weight training routine you'd probably end up with some horrible 5 day split routine. My position on well, most of BWF is that there hasn't been enough quality research on the subject. We need something like what the Soviets were doing with barbells. Overcoming Gravity had modified Prilepin's charts, Lowe suggested 4-5 sets, of 9-12s holds, based on a max of 13-18s. Seems a lot different from how people usually train them.

I've been experimenting with more high-repetition work at the moment, because I don't believe it can be as ineffective as people say, but I'm getting mixed results. I can see why people do it, especially outdoors men and soldiers, but I think I prefer low-rep work. I'll have to start trying different things with isometrics.

Another useful tool along these same lines is the German Volume Training rep tempo: super slow on the way down, explosive on the way up. I'd argue that plus maybe some pauses in the middle of the reps here and there would give about as large of a training stimulus as it's even possible to give with a given movement.

In my experience high repetition work is superior for strength building with weights, because strength is a function of hypertrophy.
